claims.text: The current feedstock consists of FeCoNiCrAl particles sized 15–45 μm.
Coatings produced from the current 15–45 μm feedstock do not consistently attain the required bond-coat thickness.
Increasing combustion-gas flow or pressure and optimizing spray distance will increase particle velocity.
Higher particle velocity increases particle kinetic energy.
Higher particle velocity increases in-flight particle heating and melting.
Enhanced melting improves splat flattening upon impact.
Improved splat flattening strengthens inter-splat bonding.
Improved melting, flattening, and inter-splat bonding increase deposition efficiency and coating-thickness accumulation.
Thermally sprayed HEA particles are susceptible to in-flight oxidation in a hot, oxygen-containing environment.
The higher-velocity particles have a shorter residence time in the oxidizing environment.
Shorter in-flight residence time reduces undesirable oxide formation.
Controlling oxygen content during deposition limits coating oxidation.
The intervention will produce a coating thicker than the stated 15–45 μm baseline.
The higher-velocity process will produce a dense, well-adhered coating.
The higher-velocity process will preserve minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
Excessive thermal input can cause undesirable phase changes in thermally sprayed HEAs.
Excessive thermal input can damage the substrate.
The resulting bond coat will remain suitable for service in a high-temperature thermal-barrier-coating system.
The quantitative thickness gain and optimal process window are not yet established and require experimental calibration.

contradictions.description: The 15–45 μm value is introduced as the feedstock particle-size range, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat it as a baseline coating-thickness range. This conflates powder size with coating thickness and leaves the actual required or baseline coating thickness unspecified.
